revisions.title: Staging an Examination
revisions.body: I hear this opening as a deliberate staging of examination. The conversation arrives through a written reconstruction; Theaetetus arrives through reports of a character in which quick learning and gentleness belong together. Socrates then shifts attention from resemblance of faces to the authority behind a judgment, and from praise to a first question about Theaetetus’s studies. The point is not yet to define knowledge, but to put a promising student—and the praise surrounding him—under scrutiny.

revisions.title: Truth at the point of contact
revisions.body: One way to hear this passage is as Socrates’ strongest local defense of Protagoras: perception is true for the perceiver because perceiver and perceived arise together in a particular encounter. The argument gains force by refusing an absolute “is.” But its final step is deliberately compressed, moving from “my perception is true for me” to “I know what I perceive.” Hear that movement as the pressure point, not as a settled conclusion.

revisions.title: The seeing–remembering test
revisions.body: Read this unit as a stress test for the equation of perception with knowledge. I take Socrates’ closing-eyes example to expose its cost: if not seeing entails not knowing, then remembering a thing would somehow erase knowledge of it. The contradiction makes the distinction between perception and knowledge unavoidable.

revisions.title: When the measure judges itself
revisions.body: I hear Socrates turn Protagoras’ measure against itself: on its own terms, the doctrine must admit that those who reject it are right, and so concede its own defeat. The proposed repair does not erase expertise; it leaves room for better judgment in health and in what benefits a city, while treating justice and piety as matters fixed by common opinion. That narrowing carries the discussion toward the next contrast, between philosophical leisure and courtroom speech.

revisions.title: Escape as likeness, not departure
revisions.body: One way to hear Socrates’ image of escape is as a change in the soul’s likeness, not a promise of leaving the human scene. The divine pattern is approached through justice, holiness, and wisdom. The philosopher is therefore not simply elsewhere; he is being asked to become like what he contemplates.

revisions.title: Testing the measure against the future
revisions.body: This stretch can be heard as a stress test for the measure doctrine: future expertise exposes the difference between feeling something now and judging what will happen. The inquiry then turns to universal motion, where even naming seems unable to hold still. I take the closing refusal as disciplined deferral, protecting the question about knowledge from being swallowed by a larger dispute.

revisions.title: The pressure inside false opinion
revisions.body: Here is the pressure I hear in this unit: the phrase “false opinion” refuses to stay simple. I take Socrates’ repeated reformulations as a deliberate tightening of the problem: each attempted account seems to leave no room for error, while the dialogue keeps insisting that error must be possible. Listen for that tension rather than treating any single proposal as the answer.

revisions.title: The wax tablet: error as misalignment
revisions.body: One way to hear this stretch is as a test of where error enters. The wax image can preserve knowledge, yet the mind may fit the right imprint to the wrong perception; error is therefore a misalignment, not mere absence. At 197b, Socrates sharpens the problem by distinguishing possessing knowledge from having it ready for use.

revisions.title: The aviary returns to the aporia
revisions.body: The aviary proposes, but does not secure, a distinction between possessing knowledge and having it at hand. Its arithmetic example makes that distinction unstable: the person who searches for knowledge may seize the wrong item, while adding ignorance only recreates the same problem. The metaphor therefore ends as a failed route back to the original aporia, not as a demonstration that possession, use, and true or false judgment cleanly come apart.

revisions.title: When true opinion is not yet knowledge
revisions.body: One way to hear this turn is as a pressure test: getting the right verdict is not yet the same as understanding why it is right. The courtroom image makes that gap vivid, and the conversation uses it to reopen the definition of knowledge. The next proposal—true opinion joined to logos—therefore arrives not as a conclusion, but as a new problem to examine.

revisions.title: The dilemma of the knowable syllable
revisions.body: I read Socrates as closing both routes by which the dream tries to separate knowledge from its elements. If a syllable is a whole made of letters, knowing the whole requires the letters, so both become knowable and expressible. If instead the syllable is a single indivisible form, it has the same status as an element: neither can be explained or known. On either reading, the promised gap between unknowable letters and knowable syllables disappears.
